chunks: LiPo trade-offs versus other batteries. The question: What are some tradeoffs of a LiPo compared to other batteries?
A LiPo (pouch) battery is a great choice when you need something light, thin or oddly shaped. But it gives up some toughness, cost and lifespan compared with other batteries.
This page is about when those trade-offs are worth it.
Think of choosing a vehicle. A sports bike is light, quick and fits through small gaps, but it is fragile and carries little.
A truck is tough and cheap per load, but heavy and bulky. A LiPo is the sports bike: it wins when weight and shape matter most.
If you need ruggedness or lowest cost, a different battery may be the better ride.
At 20 amps the pouch cell sags 0. 2 volts (3. 5 volts terminal) while the 45 milliohms cell sags 0. 9 volts (2. 8 volts, already below a 3.
0 volts cutoff) and dissipates 18 watts instead of 4 watts. The cell labelled "energy 18650" would be run at under 10 amps in practice.
Many high-drain cylindrical cells also reach 10-20 milliohms, so this is a design difference, not an inherent property of the pouch.
Energy density: stored energy per kilogram or per liter ("Li-ion chemistry in consumer electronics"). Internal resistance: the battery's own opposition to current.
Lower means more current with less heat and less voltage sag. Cycle life: how many full charge and discharge cycles before capacity falls to about 80%.
Swelling: the pouch bulging because gas forms inside as the cell ages or is abused. Pouch vs cylindrical cell: a soft foil bag versus a rigid metal can ("What LiPo stands for").
Say you need to power a thin wearable. A cylindrical can will not fit a 4 mm slot, but a pouch cell will, so the pouch wins. Now say you build a cheap, rugged power tool pack.
Cylindrical cells are made in huge numbers, are often cheaper, and survive knocks, so they win. Same chemistry family, different winner, because the need is different.
"LiPo wins on form factor, weight and energy density, with low internal resistance for high current: it can be thin and any shape.

The trade-offs: it's mechanically fragile with no hard can, it swells with age or abuse, it needs a protection circuit and careful charging like any lithium cell, cost per kWh is often higher than cylindrical cells, and cycle life and safety are worse than LiFePO4.
Versus primary lithium cells it loses on shelf life, and versus lead-acid and NiMH it loses on cost and robustness."
